tier_reason: The public rtp-benchmarks framework (uvgrtp/, ffmpeg/, live555/ senders and receivers, benchmark.pl, parse.pl) does pit uvgRTP against FFmpeg libavformat and Live555, but it publishes no results; the 4.4x goodput and 92.1% lower latency figures exist only in the MMSP 2020 abstract as seen in a search snippet, written by the uvgRTP authors themselves, and the paper (IEEE Xplore, Tampere research portal, ultravideo.fi) could not be opened. Per the snippet-only rule this caps at C.

corrections.compiler_and_flags: rtp-benchmarks Makefile builds the sender/receiver harnesses with g++ -Wall -Wextra -O2 -std=c++17 -g and links the installed uvgRTP, libavformat/libavcodec and Live555; the library versions and their build flags used for the paper are not stated in the repository.
corrections.caveats: Numbers come only from a search-result snippet of the MMSP 2020 abstract (Altonen, Räsänen, Laitinen, Viitanen, Vanne); the paper is first-party (the uvgRTP authors) and could not be opened here (IEEE Xplore, researchportal.tuni.fi and ultravideo.fi are blocked), so the percentages, test configuration and library versions were not checked against its text. The rtp-benchmarks repository carries the harness code and the hardware (Core i7-4770 and Threadripper 2990WX over a 10 Gbps LAN) but no result files or CSVs, and its README says the FFmpeg and Live555 implementations have not been tested in a while and may not work out of the box, so the comparison is not currently reproducible as published. Harness flags are -O2 -g; library build flags are not stated. Results are from 2020 library versions (uvgRTP is now at 4.0.1). The workload is RTP packetization and transport of a pre-encoded HEVC file, not encoding or decoding.

notes: Real, maintained project (BSD-2-Clause, 443 stars, last commit 2026-07-28 'Release 4.0.1') with a genuine public comparison harness, but the only numbers are a blocked first-party paper abstract seen via search snippet, so B is not supportable; could move to B only if a copy of the paper (or later ICME 2021 / ISM 2021 papers) becomes readable and confirms the figures.

tier_reason: First-party chart generated by the repo's own public CI benchmark (.github/workflows/benchmarks.yml running misc-scripts/bench-decoders.py, plotted by misc-scripts/bench-charts.py) with Makefile flags known (-march=native -std=gnu11 -O3 -flax-vector-conversions), but compiler versions are whatever the runner's apt packages provide and the CPU model of the GitHub-hosted runners is not stated, so it falls short of A.

corrections.claimed_speedup: README-benchmark.svg ('Decoding time measured on 27/07/2026 (lower is better)', median of 5 runs, all decoders single-threaded): x86-64 edge264 Clang 3.9 s, GCC 4.5 s, WASM 5.2 s, FFmpeg 4.6 s, LibAVC 6.4 s, OpenH264 8.2 s; arm64 edge264 Clang 3.8 s, GCC 3.9 s, WASM 5.0 s, FFmpeg 4.7 s, LibAVC 4.5 s, OpenH264 6.8 s. Clang build about 1.18x faster than single-threaded FFmpeg on x86-64 and 1.24x on arm64; the GCC build roughly ties FFmpeg on x86-64 (4.5 vs 4.6 s) and is about 1.2x faster on arm64 (derived from page data). FOSDEM'24 talk title linked from README: reach 10% faster speed and 3x code reduction over the state of the art.
corrections.workload: Decoding the 1080p 10 s Big Buck Bunny H.264 clip (30 MB, converted to Annex B), median of 5 runs, every decoder single-threaded: edge264_test -by (n_threads 0, YUV comparison off; wall clock via CLOCK_MONOTONIC), ffmpeg -benchmark -threads 1 -c:v h264 -f null (the script reads the utime field, i.e. user CPU time), LibAVC avcdec with --num_cores 1 (wall clock around the process), OpenH264 h264dec (its own reported time); run on GitHub-hosted runners ubuntu-latest (x86-64) and ubuntu-24.04-arm (arm64).
corrections.compiler_and_flags: Stock GCC and Clang from the runner's Ubuntu apt packages (versions not pinned or stated), make STATIC=yes with Makefile flags -march=native -std=gnu11 -O3 -flax-vector-conversions; WASM via emmake with -mrelaxed-simd under Node; FFmpeg is the Ubuntu apt package (version not stated), LibAVC built with CMake Release, OpenH264 with its default make.
corrections.hardware: GitHub-hosted runners (ubuntu-latest for x86-64, ubuntu-24.04-arm for arm64) per .github/workflows/benchmarks.yml; CPU model and core count not stated.
corrections.caveats: Numbers exist only as labels inside README-benchmark.svg, produced by the project's own CI (workflow_dispatch) on shared GitHub runners whose CPU model is not recorded; compiler and FFmpeg versions are the runner's apt defaults and are not pinned. The comparison is single-threaded only: FFmpeg is run with -threads 1, and stock edge264's multithreading is flagged experimental and is reported broken by the edge264-mvc fork, whose own chart shows multithreaded FFmpeg (2.4 s x86-64, 2.0 s arm64) beating multithreaded edge264-mvc (2.9 s, 2.6 s). Timing is asymmetric: edge264 is wall clock while the FFmpeg figure is the CLI's user CPU time (utime), which excludes system time and includes CLI demux and null-mux overhead. edge264 decodes only 8-bit 4:2:0 progressive High and MVC (no interlaced PAFF/MBAFF, no FMO, no 4:2:2/4:4:4 or high bit depth; 109/224 JVT conformance bitstreams decode), so FFmpeg is a full-featured decoder doing the same work on this progressive clip but covering far more; the benchmark disables output checking (-y). The fork documents correctness bugs in stock edge264 (SSE temporal-direct MV rounding off by up to a quarter pel, PPS scaling-matrix fall-back, high-QP 8x8 dequant overflow); whether the benchmark clip exercises them is not known. Pre-1.0, API freeze targeted for 2027.

notes: Chart labels verified by parsing the matplotlib SVG comments and their x positions (series order Clang, GCC, WASM, FFmpeg, LibAVC, OpenH264); record numbers are correct but omitted the WASM bars and the fact that FFmpeg is pinned to one thread. Metadata matches: BSD-3-Clause, 437 stars, not a fork, last commit 2026-07-28.

tier_reason: First-party chart from the fork's public CI benchmark (.github/workflows/benchmarks.yml running misc-scripts/bench-decoders.py, min of 10 runs) with Makefile flags known (-march=native -mtune=generic -std=gnu11 -O3 -flax-vector-conversions), but compiler versions are unpinned apt defaults and the runner CPU model is not stated, so not A.

corrections.claimed_speedup: Fork's README-benchmark.svg ('Decoding time measured on 19/09/2026 (lower is better)', fastest of 10 runs, all wall clock): x86-64 single-thread edge264-mvc Clang 3.9 s, GCC 4.1 s vs FFmpeg 4.8 s (about 1.23x and 1.17x faster); arm64 single-thread Clang 3.9 s, GCC 3.9 s vs FFmpeg 4.7 s (about 1.21x faster) (derived from page data). Multithreaded on all auto-detected cores: edge264-mvc Clang 2.9 s / GCC 3.0 s (x86-64) and 2.6 s / 2.6 s (arm64) vs FFmpeg 2.4 s and 2.0 s, so FFmpeg is about 1.2x (x86-64) and 1.3x (arm64) faster with threads (derived from page data). LibAVC 1T 6.7/4.4 s, MT 4.9/2.6 s; OpenH264 (single-threaded only) 8.4/6.6 s.
corrections.workload: Decoding the 1080p 10 s Big Buck Bunny H.264 clip (Annex B), fastest of 10 runs, wall-clock seconds, on GitHub-hosted runners ubuntu-latest (x86-64) and ubuntu-24.04-arm (arm64). Single-thread: edge264_test -sby, ffmpeg -threads 1, avcdec --num_cores 1. Multithread: edge264_test -mby (n_threads -1, auto-detect logical cores), ffmpeg -threads 0 (auto frame threading), avcdec --num_cores os.cpu_count(); FFmpeg read from the -benchmark rtime field.
corrections.compiler_and_flags: Stock GCC and Clang from the runner's Ubuntu apt packages (versions not stated), make STATIC=yes with Makefile flags -march=native -mtune=generic -std=gnu11 -O3 -flax-vector-conversions; FFmpeg is the Ubuntu apt package (version not stated), LibAVC built with CMake Release, OpenH264 with its default make.
corrections.hardware: GitHub-hosted runners (ubuntu-latest for x86-64, ubuntu-24.04-arm for arm64) per .github/workflows/benchmarks.yml; CPU model and core count not stated (README: the runner's few vCPUs bound the MT speedup).
corrections.caveats: Fork of tvlabs/edge264. Beyond MVC it adds working multithreaded decoding (stock edge264's experimental MT path deadlocked, emitted out of order and raced; here MT output is bit-exact to single-thread on the 231-stream JVT corpus and TSan-clean), many correctness fixes that also apply to plain AVC (SSE temporal-direct MV rounding, PPS scaling-matrix fall-back, high-QP 8x8 dequant at 32 bits), robustness fixes for real-world streams, and a -mtune=generic build default; single-threaded speed on the benchmark clip is about the same as stock (Clang 3.9 s on x86-64 in both charts). The win over FFmpeg holds only single-threaded; with all cores FFmpeg is faster on both architectures, and edge264-mvc scales from 1T to MT by only about 1.3-1.5x versus FFmpeg's 2.0-2.35x (derived from page data). CI-runner timings on shared, few-vCPU machines are noisy; the fork reports the minimum of 10 runs while stock reports the median of 5, so the two charts are not directly comparable. Same feature subset as stock (8-bit 4:2:0 progressive High and Stereo High only, no interlaced), so FFmpeg covers far more streams; the benchmark disables output checking (-y).

notes: Chart labels verified from the SVG comments and positions (series GCC-1T, GCC-MT, Clang-1T, Clang-MT, FFmpeg-1T, FFmpeg-MT, LibAVC-1T, LibAVC-MT, OpenH264); record numbers are correct (it omitted GCC-MT 3.0/2.6 s). Not a pure duplicate: it adds working multithreading and AVC correctness fixes, but its speed claim is essentially stock edge264's, so the orchestrator may prefer to fold it under edge264 as the recommended maintained fork. Metadata matches: BSD-3-Clause, 7 stars, last commit 2026-09-22.
